linkedin.text:
Every brief we receive says 'we want something memorable.'

After 16 years and 1,500+ events produced across 130+ destinations, I can tell you: that sentence is the beginning of the conversation, never the end.

Here's what I've found sitting across from HR directors, CMOs, and sales leaders before a single venue is shortlisted:

There are always two briefs.

The first is the document — the dates, the headcount, the rough budget, the vague ask for 'an experience participants will remember.'

The second brief lives underneath it. It's the real business pressure the event is meant to solve:
— A retention crisis dressed up as a team retreat.
— A post-merger culture gap dressed up as a company conference.
— A sales team running on empty dressed up as an incentive trip.
— A leadership message that isn't landing internally, dressed up as a gala dinner.

The first brief tells us what to produce. The second brief tells us what success actually looks like.

The best event directors I know — and I've worked alongside many across 130+ destinations and 25,000+ participants — are not logistics experts first. They're diagnosticians. They hold the space before the planning starts and ask: what is this event actually trying to do?

When we get that answer right, the logistics follow naturally. When we skip it and go straight to venue options and catering menus, we produce a beautiful event that solves the wrong problem.

I've seen both outcomes. The difference isn't budget. It's not venue. It's not creative concept.

It's the quality of the questions asked in the first conversation.

For anyone planning a corporate event in the next 12 months: what's the real outcome you're building toward — not the event itself, but the business result it's meant to move?

DM me or drop it in the comments. Happy to share how we'd think about it.

facebook.text:
Every event brief we receive says roughly the same thing: 'We want something memorable.'

After 1,500+ events across 130+ destinations, here's what we've learned that sentence actually means:

— The CFO wants it to justify the budget.
— The HR director wants people to stop quitting.
— The sales VP wants the team fired up for Q4.
— The CEO wants a moment the company talks about for years.

None of that is in the brief. All of it decides whether the event works.

Our job starts before the deck. It starts by asking the right questions.

What's the real outcome you're building toward? Drop it in the comments — genuinely curious.
